segments.title: CVA-01 cancellation and the advice reaching ministers
segments.body: In this criticism of CVA-01's cancellation, the search for savings outweighed defence needs because defence spending seemed to offer little electoral reward. Senior leaders had wartime experience, but a younger generation below them increasingly saw war as a theory. Junior ministers, researchers and aides determine much of the information reaching the people formally responsible for decisions. Their assumptions therefore matter alongside those of the prime minister or defence minister.

evidence.note: Political incentives, wartime experience and the advisers who prepare ministerial information.

segments.summary: The cancellation of CVA-01 raises a question about how ministers assess defence spending and whose advice shapes their decisions.

segments.title: Aircraft range versus persistent fleet air cover
segments.body: A land-based strike aircraft's ability to reach a position does not establish how long it can protect a fleet there. Transit time, the return flight and the need to replenish expended weapons all affect continuous combat air patrols. Those requirements can demand many more aircraft than a simple range circle suggests. One interpretation is that the RAF sought funding for its own programme and secured a much wider victory than it expected when carriers were cancelled. In that reading, ministers accepted the coverage claim without testing persistence or response time because it supplied the desired reason to reduce spending.

evidence.note: The RAF range-map argument, transit time, patrol rotation and weapons replenishment.

segments.summary: A range map leaves unanswered how quickly land-based aircraft can reach a fleet and how many are needed to keep fighters overhead.

segments.title: Carrier air cover protects the anti-submarine force
segments.body: The carrier argument extends beyond strike aircraft and combat air patrols. British anti-submarine doctrine relied on carriers to provide the bulk of the helicopter force, alongside the smaller detachments aboard escorts. Fighters could intercept reconnaissance aircraft before they located the fleet and provide an outer defence against air attack. They also protected anti-submarine helicopters, which could not be replaced indefinitely if enemy aircraft picked them off. Airborne early warning was another carrier capability inadequately accounted for in the cancellation argument.

evidence.note: Carrier-based ASW helicopters, reconnaissance interception, outer air defence and airborne early warning.

segments.summary: Carrier cancellation also removes the helicopter concentration, reconnaissance interception and early warning on which fleet operations depend.

segments.title: Cutting both carriers and their proposed alternative
segments.body: Long-range strike had merits of its own in this assessment. After it helped justify cancelling CVA-01, the proposed RAF capability was also cancelled, with incoming naval Buccaneers and Phantoms used as a reason that further aircraft were unnecessary. Both services consequently lost capabilities. The resulting policy concentrated on Germany and NATO while expecting allies, principally the United States, to protect British interests elsewhere. The savings depended on accepting that greater reliance.

evidence.note: The successive cancellations, transferred naval aircraft and European strategic concentration.

segments.summary: The cancellation argument ends with both services losing capabilities and Britain relying more heavily on allies beyond Europe.

segments.title: Defence spending and the cost of losing capability
segments.body: There were legitimate reasons to reform British defence spending, and retaining a force at its Second World War size was unrealistic. The criticism is that decisions increasingly followed an acceptable spending figure without first establishing the capabilities the country required. In this interpretation, the loss of defence and manufacturing independence associated with the 1990s had roots in the 1960s. A business analogy contrasts an unavoidable operating cost with a wage bill continually squeezed for savings. Defence depends on accumulated capability and experience, which makes that approach hazardous for a state.

evidence.note: Necessary postwar reform, capability versus spending and the loss of institutional experience.

segments.summary: The budget critique accepts the need for postwar reform while tracing declining independence to decisions made before the Cold War ended.

segments.title: Why Britain still needed the Invincible class
segments.body: A force without fighters faces an awkward choice when an unidentified aircraft approaches during a crisis short of war. Firing risks escalation or attacking a civilian aircraft, particularly when maritime patrol aircraft resemble airliners. Britain also needed a central platform for the anti-submarine helicopter force promised to NATO. Invincible provided the bare minimum in this assessment, despite the availability of larger designs. The criticism also extends to Type 23 and Type 45 procurement: ministers favoured the second-smallest option because it appeared economical without inviting accusations of choosing the cheapest ship. Adjusting the range of options upwards is suggested as a way to obtain the capability actually needed.

evidence.note: Aircraft identification, NATO ASW requirements and the criticism of second-smallest design choices, including Type 23 and Type 45.

segments.summary: Aircraft identification and NATO anti-submarine commitments expose the capabilities Britain still needed after cancelling its fleet carriers.

segments.title: Invincible machinery, endurance and crew
segments.body: Four Rolls-Royce Olympus TM3B gas turbines provided machinery redundancy, alongside eight Paxman Valenta diesel generators. The machinery figures are 110,000 shaft horsepower across two shafts, 28 knots, and 7,000 nautical miles at 18 knots. Displacement is 16,000 tons light and 22,000 tons fully loaded, on a hull 209 metres long with a 36-metre beam and an 8-metre draught. Later arrangements could accommodate 500 marines. A ship's company of about 650 and an air group complement of about 350 put the normal total around a thousand, much higher than estimates that count only aviation personnel.

evidence.note: Historical machinery, dimensions, endurance, troop capacity and the distinction between ship and aviation personnel.

segments.summary: The historical Invincible design combines redundant gas-turbine machinery with a crew of roughly a thousand people including its aviation personnel.

segments.title: Invincible sensors and submarine defence
segments.body: Invincible's sensors include Type 1022 air-search radar, Type 996 radar, navigation radar and Type 909 fire control for Sea Dart. Type 2016 sonar places submarine detection alongside the carrier's air and surface surveillance functions. The Royal Navy's persistent concern about underwater threats is traced to the loss of Aboukir, Cressy and Hogue. The Queen Elizabeth class lacks hull-mounted sonar but carries torpedo decoys. Those decoys suggest that it probably also has systems listening for incoming threats, although the detection fit remains uncertain here.

evidence.note: Radar and sonar fit, the Aboukir-Cressy-Hogue loss and explicitly uncertain Queen Elizabeth-class threat detection.

segments.summary: Invincible's radar and sonar fit reflects the Royal Navy's concern about submarine attack.

segments.title: Sea Dart, Goalkeeper and Phalanx on Invincible
segments.body: Invincible's armament included the original Sea Dart missile system, two 20 mm guns and three Phalanx or Goalkeeper close-in weapon systems. Goalkeeper is the preferred system in this assessment for its capabilities during the period when it was fitted. Phalanx's wider use and continuing upgrades made it the cheaper, more efficient option. The preference for Goalkeeper also rests on a theory: a less common system could attract fewer countermeasures tailored to its particular performance.

evidence.note: Original missiles and guns, alternative CIWS fits, and a qualified judgement about Goalkeeper.

segments.summary: Goalkeeper's capabilities and Phalanx's wider adoption create different reasons to favour each close-in defence system.

segments.title: Tailoring Invincible's air group
segments.body: The class's air group changed with the period and mission. Later combinations included 12 Harriers and roughly ten helicopters providing anti-submarine warfare and airborne early warning. A different mission mix could carry 18 Harriers and four Sea Kings, with a usual overall total of roughly 22 to 24 aircraft. Earlier groups used Sea Harriers, while Harrier GR7/9 and Merlin belonged to later arrangements. A 168-metre axial flight deck and 12-degree ski jump supported these aircraft on a compact but useful aviation platform.

evidence.note: Time-dependent air-group mixes, approximately 22-24 aircraft, the axial flight deck and ski jump.

segments.summary: Invincible's small flight deck supports different mixes of fighters, anti-submarine helicopters and airborne early warning aircraft.

segments.title: Deck-edge lifts and the Royal Navy's protected hangars
segments.body: Larger Invincible proposals included deck-edge lifts, with consequences for cost, ballasting, hull form and stability. Such arrangements also challenged the Royal Navy's preference for enclosed, protected hangars. Wartime enemy damage offers one explanation for that preference, but the interpretation here places greater weight on First World War experience in the North Sea. Converted seaplane carriers could lose aircraft overboard when flimsy doors or exposed deck positions failed to protect them. Missing aircraft in the records therefore need not imply unrecorded enemy action.

evidence.note: Larger designs, deck-edge lift tradeoffs and aircraft lost overboard from seaplane carriers.

segments.summary: Larger carrier options raise questions about lifts, stability and protecting parked aircraft from heavy seas.

segments.title: Why Australia and Canada needed more aviation capacity
segments.body: Bonaventure's decommissioning in 1970 places Canadian carrier replacement decisions close to the development of Invincible. Moving from a light fleet carrier to a light carrier was feasible if a country chose to retain naval aviation. In this assessment, Australian interest in the historical Invincible design was lukewarm because its aviation capability appeared insufficient. Invincible's NATO roles centred on anti-submarine support and covering reinforcement of Norway, with limited independent action against major Soviet forces. Australia and Canada needed a more versatile task-group centrepiece with more aircraft and helicopters to justify the investment.

evidence.note: Bonaventure's retirement, qualified Australian interest, NATO support roles and partner requirements.

segments.summary: An Invincible replacement had to justify itself against the task-group roles Australia and Canada expected their carriers to perform.

segments.title: Light carriers and middle-power independence
segments.body: A replacement carrier had to support convoy protection, allied task-group leadership and some independent power projection. Earlier light fleet carriers had given Australia and Canada a foreign-policy presence beyond what their defence spending alone suggested. Britain could also signal intent with a carrier, but its nuclear weapons supplied another level of national power. For Australia and Canada, carriers were their strongest naval demonstration of commitment. A useful successor therefore needed enough capability to carry that diplomatic and operational weight.

evidence.note: Convoy protection, independent power projection and carriers as a middle-power contribution to alliances.

segments.summary: For Australia and Canada, carrier aviation offered task-group leadership and a stronger voice in allied operations.

segments.title: V/STOL aircraft and catapult airframe loads
segments.body: Joining the Invincible programme in this period also meant committing to Sea Harrier. British V/STOL development made operation from a relatively short deck possible without catapults and arrested recovery. The airframe still needed strength, but its launch forces came from its own propulsion. Catapult launches imposed external pulling loads, while arrested landings imposed severe deceleration through the recovery system. These differences affected the structural demands placed on the aircraft.

evidence.note: Sea Harrier programme dependence and the structural difference between V/STOL and catapult launch and recovery.

segments.summary: The Sea Harrier made a short carrier deck useful while avoiding the launch and recovery loads imposed by catapults and arresting gear.

segments.title: Sea Harrier capability within procurement constraints
segments.body: The early Sea Harrier offered a reasonably capable radar and useful combat air patrol capability, with adequate range and a limited strike role. The later Sea Harrier 2 was more capable, although it belonged to a period well after the Falklands War. A fully equipped conventional carrier would offer another option in an ideal procurement setting. Returning to that option after publicly declaring such ships unnecessary would require politicians to admit a mistake. Equipment selection also involves affordability, domestic or allied production and internal government compromise, so the chosen system need not represent a purely technical optimum.

evidence.note: Early and later Sea Harrier capability, political reluctance to reverse retirement decisions and procurement compromises.

segments.summary: Sea Harrier supplied a useful air-defence and strike capability within political limits on rebuilding conventional carrier aviation.

segments.title: Gun ammunition, RAM missiles and the cost of close defence
segments.body: Naval interest in laser close defence may partly reflect reluctance to revisit earlier decisions about guns. Moving to Rolling Airframe Missiles had already been presented as making gun systems unnecessary. The illustrative prices are about $5,000 for a 57 mm round and roughly 84 times that amount for a RAM missile. RAM can be inexpensive relative to a Standard missile while remaining expensive beside gun ammunition.

evidence.note: Interest in laser close defence and the illustrative 57 mm ammunition and RAM cost comparison.

segments.summary: An illustrative ammunition-cost comparison supports retaining guns alongside missile defences.

segments.title: Layered air defence and different gun ranges
segments.body: Second World War formations combined 20 mm Oerlikons and 40 mm Bofors with heavier weapons, including 4-inch, 4.5-inch and 5.25-inch guns, as well as fighter protection. Different calibres supplied overlapping defensive layers. In the Pacific, Japanese aircraft could circle beyond the expected reach of American 5-inch/38 guns, especially when the formation lacked carrier fighters to intercept them. British 5.25-inch guns could reach farther. Gunners could let the aircraft settle into that apparent safe distance before opening fire. Sea Harriers would supply another defensive layer beyond the ships' own weapons.

evidence.note: Mixed anti-aircraft calibres, aircraft circling beyond 5-inch/38 range without opposing carrier fighters, and the additional reach of 5.25-inch guns.

segments.summary: Different gun ranges and fighter cover gave fleets overlapping defences, including a way to engage aircraft circling beyond American 5-inch/38 range.

segments.title: Helicopter early warning and the Falklands funding decision
segments.body: The rapid introduction of helicopter airborne early warning during the Falklands War depended on research completed years earlier. Funding had been withheld because British ships were expected to operate in the NATO North Atlantic area. American carrier aircraft and land-based airborne warning were assumed to provide the necessary coverage there. The wartime work that equipped Illustrious before she sailed south therefore put an existing development into service.

evidence.note: Earlier AEW development, deferred implementation and reliance on allied and land-based coverage.

segments.summary: Previously completed research allowed helicopter airborne early warning to enter service quickly during the Falklands War.

segments.title: Choosing a carrier air group for its intended jobs
segments.body: Sea Kings offer anti-submarine warfare, commando transport and other helicopter tasks. Adding Sea Harriers brings strike and air defence, with later reconnaissance pods extending the aircraft's uses. These capabilities remain useful despite their limited reach. Comparing headline performance figures alone cannot establish whether an aircraft or warship suits a particular navy. A procurement decision needs to consider the jobs the force intends to perform and the capabilities it lacks. The enlarged air group proposed for Britain and its partners needs to meet those requirements.

evidence.note: Helicopter and Harrier capabilities, limited range and matching purchases to operational requirements.

segments.summary: Sea Kings and Sea Harriers illustrate why procurement needs to account for a navy's missions and existing capability gaps.

segments.title: Gorshkov and Soviet ocean-going naval power
segments.body: Kirov was laid down in 1974, launched in 1977 and commissioned in 1980. Kiev followed a different timetable: laid down in 1970, launched in 1972 and commissioned in 1975. Both belong to the expansion of Soviet ocean-going capability associated with Sergey Gorshkov, who remained in office until 1985. He was willing to let others receive credit when their actions advanced his aims. One explanation for his political durability is his willingness to remain in his naval position without pursuing the highest political office.

evidence.note: Kirov and Kiev construction dates, Gorshkov's tenure and an interpretation of his political methods.

segments.summary: Kirov and Kiev entered service during Soviet naval expansion under Sergey Gorshkov.

segments.title: Soviet deployments and the cost of diverting NATO forces
segments.body: Invincible, Illustrious and Ark Royal entered construction and service during the same broad period as the Soviet Navy's larger ocean-going ships. Invincible was laid down in 1973 and commissioned in 1980, followed into service by Illustrious in 1982 and Ark Royal in 1985. Kirovs and Kievs would probably serve primarily around Soviet naval bastions, but their ability to operate elsewhere still required a response. An attack submarine could pursue one, at the cost of removing that submarine from the North Atlantic campaign. Diverting an American carrier battle group would create a similar absence in the North Atlantic or North Pacific. A deployment in the Indian Ocean could therefore affect the balance in the main theatres.

evidence.note: Invincible-class dates, Soviet bastion roles and the opportunity cost of responding to distant surface units.

segments.summary: A distant Soviet surface deployment could draw submarines or a carrier group away from the main North Atlantic and North Pacific campaigns.

segments.title: Surface raiders and diversion from a decisive theatre
segments.body: A Soviet intelligence-history unit spent most of two decades recovering, translating and evaluating German surface-raider reports. Its conclusion was that a raider becomes useful when the response draws sufficient enemy strength away from a critical theatre. The Soviet assessment treated the Second World War as a weaker general example because much of the surface raiding occurred in areas already considered critical. The First World War supplied the example of two British battlecruisers sent to the Falkland Islands in response to German armoured cruisers. Early in the Second World War, the hunt for Graf Spee also committed substantial forces, including Ark Royal, Renown and cruisers. Germany still needed to exploit the opportunities those diversions created. In a Cold War conflict of uncertain duration, keeping enemy units occupied elsewhere could reduce the forces available against the main Soviet effort.

evidence.note: Soviet study of German raiding, its comparison of the two world wars, the Falklands battlecruiser diversion and forces committed to hunting Graf Spee.

segments.summary: German raiding operations illustrate how a threat overseas can draw an opponent's scarce major warships away from a critical front.

segments.title: Combining Soviet surface raiders with submarines
segments.body: Knowledge of Soviet interest in surface raiding left the allies with a planning problem. The threat could be a bluff, but the developing Soviet force made it practical enough to require preparation. A distant operation would not necessarily need a Kirov or Kiev. Other cruisers could reinforce submarines already operating overseas and use their helicopters for reconnaissance. Surface guns could also attack suitable targets with ammunition cheaper and easier to replenish than torpedoes or missiles.

evidence.note: Uncertain Soviet intentions, smaller cruiser deployments, helicopter reconnaissance and replenishment of gun ammunition.

segments.summary: A feasible Soviet raiding option creates a planning problem even when the allies cannot be certain it will be used.

segments.title: The counterfactual decision to defend Atlantic reinforcements
segments.body: The Royal Navy had responded to the Sverdlov cruisers by building carriers and Buccaneer strike aircraft. In the counterfactual, Britain gives protection of sea communications a stronger place alongside its commitment to the European front. American and Canadian reinforcements, equipment and supplies must be able to cross the North Atlantic. This assumes a war that continues long enough for reinforcement and resupply to matter. Submarines contribute to that protection, but they can miss a target or be required elsewhere. Carrier strike aircraft provide an additional response when the submarine force cannot meet every threat.

evidence.note: Sverdlov and Buccaneer precedent, sustained Atlantic reinforcement and carrier strikes supplementing submarines.

segments.summary: The enlarged-carrier scenario begins with Britain preparing for a sustained war and protecting the reinforcement traffic needed to fight it.

segments.title: Sea Eagle missiles and a larger Sea Harrier strike
segments.body: The 580 kg Sea Eagle has a 230 kg warhead, a length of 4.14 metres and a 1.2-metre wingspan. Its quoted turbojet performance is more than 110 km of range at around Mach 1. It uses inertial guidance and active radar homing and can fly low. Continued development would probably have kept the weapon useful into the present. A larger Sea Harrier force could launch more missiles against an opposing surface ship. Whether that attack would overwhelm a Kiev or Kirov remains uncertain.

evidence.note: Missile dimensions, quoted performance, guidance and explicit uncertainty about overwhelming Kiev or Kirov.

segments.summary: Sea Eagle's guidance and warhead support the proposed anti-ship role, while the chance of overwhelming Soviet defences remains uncertain.

segments.title: Submarine pursuit cannot guarantee a timely interception
segments.body: The Falklands cruiser sinking supplies an example of the destructive result of several Mark VIII torpedo hits. Delivering such an attack still requires a submarine to find the target and reach a useful firing position. A surface ship travelling at 20 knots can force a pursuing submarine to make substantially more speed to catch it. At the illustrative 25 knots, rapid movement through the water creates noise and compromises the submarine's stealth. That becomes a problem when convoys are already threatened and available submarines are out of position. The counterfactual carriers supply another way to respond rapidly, including in distant waters such as the Indian Ocean. Indian participation is briefly considered alongside Britain, Australia and Canada.

evidence.note: Mark VIII torpedoes in the Falklands cruiser example, submarine positioning and pursuit noise, convoy threats and possible Indian participation.

segments.summary: A submarine waiting in position has different advantages from one racing to catch a fast-moving surface ship.

segments.title: Prewar submarine deployments and bastion barriers
segments.body: One Cold War concept would place allied submarines around Soviet bastions to intercept submarines leaving them after war began. Soviet boats could instead depart before that barrier became an active wartime interception line. Following them would risk opening gaps in the patrol arrangement, while attacking them early would start the conflict. The open sea provides much more freedom of movement than a defended land border. Territorial waters occupy only a small part of the operational space, making prewar positioning difficult to control.

evidence.note: Departures before hostilities and the resulting pursuit, patrol-gap and escalation dilemmas.

segments.summary: A barrier intended to intercept submarines at the outbreak of war faces a different problem if they sail before hostilities begin.

segments.title: The maximum Invincible hull and propulsion arrangement
segments.body: The enlarged carrier is compared with Kiev's approximately 42,000 to 45,000-ton full-load displacement, but would omit Kiev's large forward anti-ship missile battery. Its proposed dimensions are 255 metres long, a 44-metre beam and a 9.8-metre draught. The machinery list contains six Rolls-Royce Olympus TM3B gas turbines and 12 Paxman diesel generators. The propulsion proposal produces 150,000 shaft horsepower across three shafts for a maximum speed of 32 knots. Increased fuel storage is intended to permit 8,000 nautical miles at 18 knots. These are proposed specifications for the counterfactual ship.

evidence.note: Counterfactual dimensions, machinery, power, speed and endurance, with the clear Kiev size comparison.

segments.summary: The hypothetical enlargement approaches Kiev in scale, with additional gas turbines and fuel capacity supporting a larger carrier.

segments.title: Crewing and self-defence for the enlarged carrier
segments.body: The initial personnel estimate is about 750 in the ship's company, 450 in the air group and capacity for up to 500 marines. The air-group figure is deliberately conservative and could be closer to 600. The estimate aims to keep the cost of additional personnel as low as possible. Gas-turbine machinery is part of the reason the ship's company would grow less quickly than the hull and aviation capacity. The proposed weapons include Sea Dart, Sea Wolf and 20 mm anti-aircraft guns. Phalanx or Goalkeeper would probably arrive after the Falklands War, with no firm assumption of earlier fitting. The existing radar and sonar approach is retained.

evidence.note: Qualified personnel estimates, proposed missile and gun fit, post-Falklands CIWS and retained sensors.

segments.summary: Restrained crewing estimates accompany an enlarged carrier that retains the Invincible family's sensors and adds Sea Wolf.

segments.title: The enlarged carrier's baseline air group
segments.body: The nominal group contains 24 Sea Harriers, 20 Sea King HAS.2 anti-submarine helicopters and four Sea King AEW.2 helicopters. That gives a total of 48 aircraft. An alternative allocation exchanges two anti-submarine helicopters for two more early warning aircraft. The larger deck and probable deck-edge lifts are estimated to accommodate at least 54 to 56 aircraft, leaving room to consider further early warning helicopters. The initial 48-aircraft allocation is deliberately conservative.

evidence.note: The 24/20/4 baseline, alternative 24/18/6 mix and tentative larger deck capacity.

segments.summary: The conservative proposal provides 24 fighters and more space for anti-submarine and early warning helicopters.

segments.title: Sustaining a fighter patrol and airborne early warning
segments.body: The working minimum for maintaining a four-aircraft package is 18 aircraft. The proposed cycle puts four fighters and one airborne early warning helicopter in the air, another group ready on deck, and another at hangar alert. The remaining airframes rotate through maintenance and preparation. Twenty-four Sea Harriers, organised as two squadrons, provide more depth than that minimum. Increasing the helicopter force to 24 anti-submarine Sea Kings and six early warning aircraft would produce a 54-aircraft group.

evidence.note: Airborne, deck-alert and hangar-alert cycles, with a possible 54-aircraft group.

segments.summary: A larger Sea Harrier force supports a continuous four-aircraft patrol while keeping replacements ready and allowing for maintenance.

segments.title: A larger air group for sea control
segments.body: Increasing each fighter squadron from 12 to 16 aircraft would put 32 Sea Harriers aboard. With deck-edge lifts and some deck parking, the theoretical upper combination is 32 fighters, 24 anti-submarine Sea Kings and six early warning Sea Kings, totalling 62 aircraft. The conservative 48-aircraft proposal limits additional spending. Its principal tasks remain command, presence and leadership of anti-submarine warfare, supported by air defence, reconnaissance and limited strikes. The design would still have less capability than a full fleet carrier.

evidence.note: The theoretical 62-aircraft combination, conservative baseline and intended sea-control roles.

segments.summary: Additional aircraft and deck parking could give the enlarged carrier a stronger sea-control force with limited strike capability.

segments.title: A longer flight deck improves Harrier operations
segments.body: The historical Invincible has an approximately 209-metre hull and a 168-metre axial flight deck. Applying the same 41-metre difference to the proposed 255-metre ship leaves about 214 metres of flight deck. That additional run could support heavier takeoff loads or more efficient departures. It also creates more scope for a rolling landing, if that operating method is adopted.

evidence.note: A 214-metre flight deck is estimated by applying the historical hull-to-deck length difference.

segments.summary: The proposed 255-metre hull provides more takeoff distance and room to consider rolling landings.

segments.title: Launching a rapid anti-shipping strike
segments.body: Six additional Harriers could remain configured with Sea Eagle and Sidewinder missiles while the carrier maintains its fighter alert. Launching them with four covering fighters would produce a ten-aircraft package. A ski-jump departure allows the next aircraft to follow once the previous aircraft has cleared the ramp, without resetting a catapult. This arrangement suits a relatively small strike whose mission does not demand a heavy bomb load at very long range. Against a Kirov-type threat, aircraft could approach at low level through radar clutter before launching anti-ship missiles, following the same principle as the planned Buccaneer tactics. The proposed carrier would still have less reach than a CATOBAR carrier.

evidence.note: Six strike aircraft plus four covering fighters, consecutive ski-jump launches and low-level missile attacks.

segments.summary: Six strike-configured Sea Harriers and four covering fighters form a small anti-shipping package suited to rapid ski-jump launches.

segments.title: Damage can end a surface raider's freedom
segments.body: A surface raider operating far from support becomes especially vulnerable after sustaining damage. Graf Spee's arrival at Montevideo illustrates the problem: its location was known while Ark Royal and Renown were approaching. A crew cannot rapidly replace home-country industrial support, repair facilities or unavailable spare parts. In the proposed anti-shipping mission, even an attack that fails to sink its target could therefore constrain the raider's operations. Some attacking Harriers and their pilots could be lost. That risk has to be weighed against leaving a Kirov or Udaloy free to continue causing damage.

evidence.note: Graf Spee at Montevideo, repair limitations and the choice between risking attacking Harriers and leaving hostile surface ships free to operate.

segments.summary: Graf Spee illustrates how damage constrains a raider without repair facilities, spare parts or a secure destination.

segments.title: Eight carriers change Sea Harrier production
segments.body: Assigning two 12-aircraft squadrons to each of eight carriers creates 16 active squadrons. Procurement would probably exceed 300 Sea Harriers once the supporting organisation is included. Each participating country would need training and maintenance capacity as well as its operational aircraft. The comparison's historical baseline is 98 Sea Harriers.

evidence.note: The projected order exceeds 300 aircraft for 16 operational squadrons plus national support requirements.

segments.summary: A joint carrier fleet requires a much larger Sea Harrier purchase once national training and maintenance needs are included.

segments.title: Maritime trade and the need to protect sea routes
segments.body: Canadian and Australian carrier operations would help protect the sea lines of communication on which both countries depend. Japan's naval strength follows the same concern for maritime access. Disruption around maritime chokepoints, Red Sea shipping and piracy illustrate why a country needs to contribute forces if it expects its interests to count. The quoted estimates attribute an overwhelming share of trade to sea transport, but vary by both volume and value without settling on a precise percentage. Undersea cables carrying most internet data add another dependence on maritime infrastructure. Avoiding the protection bill leaves valuable trade and communications exposed to people willing to reach them.

evidence.note: National responsibility for sea routes, rough trade estimates, piracy and undersea data cables.

segments.summary: Canada's and Australia's reasons for operating carriers rest on their dependence on trade routes and maritime communications.

segments.title: A multinational market for helicopter early warning
segments.body: Joint procurement would probably bring Sea King airborne early warning into service before the Falklands War. Four aircraft per carrier, with supporting airframes, could produce a fleet of at least 48; six per carrier raises the projected total to 72 including spares. The larger estimate allocates about 36 to Britain and 18 each to Australia and Canada. Several operators would share the incentive to maintain and improve the system. US amphibious groups already operating Harriers could become interested in the early warning equipment or concept without necessarily adopting the Sea King airframe. Wider use would lower the cost of entry while the system retained its usefulness. Helicopter early warning would remain an additional option for ships unable to operate fixed-wing aircraft, with less capability than Hawkeye or E-3 aircraft.

evidence.note: Earlier adoption, alternative 48- and 72-airframe fleets, national support shares and possible US interest in the early warning system without the Sea King airframe.

segments.summary: Orders from several navies could bring helicopter early warning into service earlier and support continued development.

segments.title: More aircraft allow a stronger alert force
segments.body: The preferred expanded group combines 32 Sea Harriers, 24 anti-submarine helicopters and six airborne early warning helicopters. Thirty-two fighters would not guarantee a permanently available strike force alongside the patrol, but they allow a strike group on deck and additional aircraft ready in the hangar. A 12-aircraft strike could then become practical against a major threat. Six early warning helicopters make it easier to keep one airborne and another ready while sustaining the four-fighter patrol.

evidence.note: The preferred 32/24/6 group and its effect on strike readiness and continuous early warning.

segments.summary: Thirty-two fighters and six early warning helicopters give the enlarged carrier more options for simultaneous patrols and strikes.

segments.title: Interchangeable helicopter mission equipment
segments.body: Six early warning helicopters would allow periods with two aircraft airborne when the threat increased. A more configurable system could also permit an anti-submarine helicopter to exchange its mission equipment for early warning equipment while at sea. Interchangeable airframes and removable mission pods were considered repeatedly, especially in connection with Merlin. The proposal was abandoned because it did not appear economically sensible or viable. Additional international partners are a possible reason for pursuing greater flexibility in the counterfactual programme.

evidence.note: Surging two AEW aircraft, exchanging mission equipment and the historical rejection of interchangeable airframes.

segments.summary: A larger helicopter fleet raises the possibility of reinforcing early warning by exchanging mission equipment aboard anti-submarine airframes.

segments.title: Why larger carriers might not prevent the Falklands War
segments.body: The economic case for deterrence is that funding ships which prevent war costs less than fighting the war and having to build the ships anyway. Even with four larger British carriers ordered, the complete force would not enter service until 1987. The scenario assumes that diplomatic neglect continues, including failures to heed the governor and the ambassador in Buenos Aires. More naval capability therefore does not guarantee that the Falklands War is prevented.

evidence.note: The preference for successful deterrence, 1987 delivery of the complete force and unchanged diplomatic failures.

segments.summary: Carrier delivery dates and diplomatic decisions leave room for war even with a larger British fleet on order.

segments.title: More Sea Harriers could reduce Falklands losses
segments.body: Depending on loading, the hypothetical force could take 40 or more Sea Harriers south, with estimates reaching 48 or 52. Forty aircraft with airborne early warning would make two four-aircraft combat air patrols easier to sustain, while 52 approaches the capacity for three daytime patrols and one overnight. The limited pattern of Argentine night attacks would leave more opportunity for aircraft maintenance. Even a 28-aircraft Sea Harrier force could maintain a patrol, alert fighters and surge capacity with airborne early warning. Ground-attack Harriers could add laser-guided bombing capability. Ship losses could fall by half or even be eliminated, although additional carriers and aircraft would not solve every problem. Avoiding the Sir Galahad disaster or the container-ship loss would also preserve logistics assets and change the campaign's support.

evidence.note: Hypothetical fighter totals, the benefit of AEW even with 28 Sea Harriers, multiple patrols, qualified reductions in losses and preservation of logistics shipping.

segments.summary: A larger fighter force with early warning could sustain more patrols and help preserve ships and supplies needed ashore.

segments.title: Early warning changes the Argentine fuel problem
segments.body: Twelve airborne early warning helicopters would make it practical to maintain two airborne continuously in the scenario. Positioning one north of the islands and one south would offer warning of approaching aircraft at greater distances. Attackers could try to evade detection by flying low and slowly, but those profiles would consume fuel less efficiently. Reduced fuel margins mean less range, less time over the target and fewer aircraft able to participate. The same surveillance could also close down Argentine night resupply flights sooner.

evidence.note: Two AEW helicopters around the islands and the proposed fuel, range and resupply consequences of radar evasion.

segments.summary: Helicopters north and south of the Falklands could force attackers into less efficient approaches and reduce their operating options.

segments.title: Export prospects for the enlarged Invincible
segments.body: At 255 metres, the enlarged Invincible would still be almost 30 metres shorter than the 284-metre Queen Elizabeth class. The programme could nevertheless encourage a larger or more international successor design. Two Canadian ships would suit a force concentrated on the Atlantic coast, while Australia could seek more than its initial pair. India and possibly Japan could also join during the 1980s. The attraction would be a modern aviation capability with less dependence on another country's specialist carrier infrastructure.

evidence.note: Length comparison, Canadian Atlantic basing and possible additional customers.

segments.summary: The enlarged Invincible remains smaller than Queen Elizabeth while offering a possible shared design for several navies.

segments.title: The infrastructure cost of CATOBAR independence
segments.body: France's reliance on American catapult infrastructure illustrates the cost of supporting CATOBAR operations at limited national production scale. Maintenance facilities and supporting systems are expensive to establish, and rebuilding them after abandonment is especially difficult. Successive government design changes added cost to the Queen Elizabeth programme, while treating the catapult choice like an optional fitting overlooked the infrastructure required. Complete national infrastructure would buy logistical and political independence at a higher price. A cheaper system could create greater dependence, leaving governments inclined toward compromises between the two.

evidence.note: French catapult dependence, sustaining versus regenerating infrastructure and cost-versus-independence choices.

segments.summary: Choosing catapults requires a support system whose cost and political dependencies extend beyond the carrier.

segments.title: Australia and Japan could extend the joint programme
segments.body: In this scenario, Australia would probably acquire three carriers, while Britain would retain four and could add a fifth after the Falklands War. India and Japan would likely become involved at some level. Japan might develop its own ship while adopting the Sea Harrier system and possibly producing the aircraft domestically. That possibility depends on more serious attention to sea-route threats and a sufficiently attractive cost of entry. The ships would be perceived differently from traditional carriers, which could affect their reception in Japan. This would bring Japan into that form of naval aviation earlier than the Izumo programme.

evidence.note: Tentative fleet expansion and Japanese local development, tied to threat perception, affordability and classification, with an earlier start than the Izumo programme.

segments.summary: Greater concern for trade-route security could encourage additional carriers and a Japanese route into Sea Harrier operations.

segments.title: Joint procurement and carriers for the F-35B
segments.body: The Treasury had justified a two-ship limit with an availability study, while allowing the carrier size to vary. Replacing an established international fleet would change that argument over how many new British carriers were needed. Continuing Canadian or Australian participation could spread costs and make additional British ships more likely. Canada is not expected to build its own carriers, while Australia might accept British-built hulls and complete the fitting out locally, following the comparison with the Canberra class. A ship without steam or electromagnetic catapults would avoid some demanding installation and calibration work. The enlarged Invincible design would also provide more practical capacity for independent operations. Those differences could carry into the later F-35B programme.

evidence.note: The Treasury's two-ship availability argument, international replacement procurement, Australian fitting out and practical independence with the later F-35B.

segments.summary: Continuing international participation could change replacement-carrier numbers, construction arrangements and practical independence.
